name: Lachen

local_name.name: Lachen
local_name.meaning: big pass, as against Lachung, the small pass

tagline: Gurudongmar's base village, run by its own Dzumsa
meta_description: Lachen, North Sikkim: Dzumsa village at 2,750 m and base for Gurudongmar Lake. 2026 road status, permits, hotels, homestays, prices and altitude advice.
summary: Lachen is a Bhutia village at about 2,750 m in the Lachen Chu valley, roughly 120 km and 5–6 hours from Gangtok. It is the overnight stop before Gurudongmar Lake, governed by its own Dzumsa council, with an 1858 Nyingma monastery. Reopened in September 2026 after long closures; check current status before you travel.
intro: Lachen sits on a shelf above the Lachen Chu, a few hours' drive up the valley from Chungthang. Older wooden houses with carved windows climb the slope above the road, the monastery stands at the top of the village, and the hotels cluster along the highway. Beyond Lachen the valley rises to Thangu, the high pastures and the plateau country around Gurudongmar Lake, which is why almost every visitor spends just one short night here.

Like Lachung, Lachen governs itself through the Dzumsa, the village council of its Bhutia households, led by an elected Pipon with assistants called Gyenbo. Lachen people have long ties with the high pastures, and with the Dokpa herders who graze yak and sheep in the Lashar and Lhonak valleys to the north. Ask your host about the summer and winter moves of the herds.

Lachen has been hard hit in recent years. The October 2023 South Lhonak flood tore through the valley below at Chungthang, and landslides closed the road through much of 2024–26. As we understand it, Lachen reopened on 9 March 2026 over a new Bailey bridge on the Taram Chu, closed again in April, and permits resumed around 11–12 September 2026. Check current status before you travel.

story.title: The Frenchwoman and the hermit of Lachen
story.text: In late May 1912 a French scholar of Buddhism, Alexandra David-Néel, arrived in Lachen and met the Lachen Gomchen Rinpoche, the hermit lama and superior of the village monastery. According to Wikipedia's account of her life, drawn from her own writings and biographies, she stayed in and around Lachen on and off for several years, living for long periods in a cave hermitage at about 4,000 m above the village. The Gomchen taught her meditation and Tibetan practices, and gave her the religious name Yeshe Tome, Lamp of Wisdom. Sidkeong Tulku Namgyal, the crown prince who briefly became Chogyal of Sikkim in 1914, visited them at Lachen, and the three discussed reforming Buddhism in the kingdom. From her retreat near Lachen she slipped across the border into Tibet in 1916, without permission, to visit Tashilhunpo, and the British authorities expelled her from Sikkim on her return. Years later, in 1924, she reached Lhasa in disguise and became famous in Europe. Her Tibetan journey began in this village, with a hermit most visitors have never heard of.
story.source: Wikipedia, Alexandra David-Néel; David-Néel, My Journey to Lhasa (1927)

little_known.fact: Lachen Monastery, also called Ngodrub Choling, was built in 1858 and belongs to the Nyingma school; it houses the Lachen Monastic School.
After a review by a state committee in 2001, the shrine building at Gurudongmar Lake was handed to Lachen Monastery, which keeps a lama there as caretaker.
Lachen's Dzumsa is led by the Pipon and assistants called Gyenbo, and Sikkim law has recognised it as the village's local government since the 1990s.

facts: Gurudongmar base, Dzumsa council, 1858 monastery, yak country
Protected area permit via a registered agent; Indians only beyond Thangu

highlights.title: Lachen Monastery
highlights.text: Ngodrub Choling, a Nyingma monastery built in 1858 at the top of the village, with a monastic school and wide views down the valley. Its Gomchen (hermit lama) taught Alexandra David-Néel in the 1910s, and the monastery looks after the shrine at Gurudongmar Lake.

highlights.title: Gateway to Gurudongmar
highlights.text: Lachen is the last sensible night before Gurudongmar Lake, about 67 km and 3–3.5 hours further. Vehicles leave at 4–5 am. Eat early, sleep early and keep warm clothes ready the night before.

highlights.title: The old village above the road
highlights.text: Above the hotels, Lachen's older houses of wood and stone, prayer flags and stacked firewood show how the village lived before tourism. A short walk at dusk, with permission, gives a sense of a working high village.

highlights.title: Yak and herder country
highlights.text: North of Lachen lie the summer pastures of Thangu, Chopta, Lashar and Lhonak, where Lachenpa and Dokpa herders keep yak and sheep. You may pass herds on the Gurudongmar road; ask before photographing herders.

highlights.title: Thangu and Chopta beyond
highlights.text: About 30 km above Lachen, Thangu village at about 3,900 m is the breakfast stop on the way to the lake, and Chopta Valley nearby is a high meadow that flowers in summer and freezes in winter.

how_to_reach.text: Most visitors join a shared 2N/3D Lachen–Lachung package from Gangtok, with permit, simple stays and meals. Jeeps leave Gangtok around 10–11 am and reach Lachen late afternoon.
A private registered SUV takes 5–6 hours for about 120 km via Mangan and Chungthang. Your agent handles the permit. Vehicles must cross the Toong check post by 4:00 pm.
Drive 4.5–5 hours to Gangtok on NH10, or via Kalimpong or Algarah when NH10 is closed, and spend a night there before heading north. A same-day transfer to Lachen is not possible.

costs: ≈ ₹1,500–3,000 a room, or ₹1,200–2,000 pp with meals
where_to_stay: Lachen has a small range of hotels along the highway and family homestays in the older village above. On a budget, a Lachenpa homestay with dinner and an early breakfast costs about ₹1,200–2,000 per person. Summit Gangchen, run by the Sikkim-based Summit group, is the largest and best-equipped hotel, with heated beds, and is our comfort choice before the cold Gurudongmar morning. Capacity is limited since the 2026 reopening, so book early.
tips: Lay out warm clothes and documents the night before; you leave for Gurudongmar at 4–5 am.
Skip alcohol in Lachen; it worsens altitude symptoms at the lake next morning.
Carry a refillable bottle; Lachen has restricted packaged water bottles at times.
Children under five are not permitted in North Sikkim protected areas.
Foreign nationals: rules for Lachen and Thangu are unclear, so ask us first.

experiences.title: Ngodrub Choling, Lachen's monastery
experiences.best_time: Late afternoon on arrival, or after Gurudongmar
experiences.cost: Free; a small offering is welcome
experiences.summary: Climb to Lachen Monastery, built in 1858, for its murals, its monastic school and a wide view down the Lachen valley. This is the monastery whose Gomchen taught Alexandra David-Néel, and which cares for the shrine at Gurudongmar Lake.
body: Lachen Monastery, known as Ngodrub Choling, stands at the top of the village, a short drive or a steep 15–20 minute walk from the highway hotels. Built in 1858, it belongs to the Nyingma school, the oldest of the Tibetan Buddhist traditions and the one most closely tied to Guru Padmasambhava. A monastic school trains young monks here.

Visit on arrival in the late afternoon if you reach Lachen with light to spare, or on the way back from Gurudongmar if your schedule allows. Walk clockwise around the building, remove shoes and hats inside, and ask before taking photographs. If prayers are under way, wait quietly or watch from the door.

The monastery also links the village to its two best-known stories. Its Gomchen, or hermit lama, taught the French scholar Alexandra David-Néel in the 1910s. And since 2001 it has looked after the shrine building at Gurudongmar Lake, where it keeps a lama as caretaker.

faqs.q: When was Lachen Monastery built?
faqs.a: In 1858, according to Wikipedia's article on the monastery. It is a Nyingma monastery, known as Ngodrub Choling, and houses the Lachen Monastic School. The present buildings have been renovated over the years, and the monastery remains the spiritual centre of the village.

faqs.q: Is there time to visit Lachen Monastery on a package?
faqs.a: Often, if you arrive in Lachen by about 4 pm. Most packages reach Lachen late afternoon and leave before dawn, so the evening of arrival is your window. Ask your driver to take you up for half an hour. On some itineraries a visit fits after Gurudongmar, before lunch.

faqs.q: Can we photograph inside Lachen Monastery?
faqs.a: Ask first. Many Sikkim monasteries do not allow photography inside the prayer hall, and rules vary. Exteriors and views are usually fine. Never photograph monks at prayer without permission, and do not use flash.

experiences.title: The hermit of Lachen and Alexandra David-Néel
experiences.summary: Hear the story of the French scholar who studied with the Lachen Gomchen from 1912, lived in a cave hermitage above the village, and slipped into Tibet from here in 1916. A story most Gurudongmar visitors never learn.
body: Alexandra David-Néel came to Sikkim in 1912 to study Buddhism and befriended the crown prince, Sidkeong Tulku Namgyal. In late May that year she reached Lachen and met its Gomchen, the hermit lama of the monastery. She stayed near Lachen on and off for several years, often in a cave hermitage at about 4,000 m, practising meditation under his guidance.

The Gomchen gave her the name Yeshe Tome, Lamp of Wisdom. From her retreat near Lachen she crossed into Tibet in July 1916, without permission, to visit Tashilhunpo near Shigatse, and the British expelled her from Sikkim on her return. In 1924 she reached Lhasa in disguise, and her book My Journey to Lhasa made her famous.

We tell this story on the evening in Lachen, and a local host can sometimes add what the village remembers. The cave itself is not a tourist site and lies in restricted, high terrain, so we do not take visitors there. The point is to see Lachen as more than a stop before the lake.

faqs.q: Who was Alexandra David-Néel?
faqs.a: A French explorer, writer and scholar of Buddhism, born in 1868, who studied in Sikkim from 1912, including with the Lachen Gomchen, and in 1924 reached Lhasa in disguise. Her book My Journey to Lhasa, published in 1927, made her famous. She died in 1969.

faqs.q: Can we visit David-Néel's cave near Lachen?
faqs.a: No, not as a tourist outing. The hermitage lies in high, restricted terrain above the village, and there is no regular route or permit for visitors. We share the story in Lachen instead. Some books about her life describe the site in detail.

faqs.q: What books tell the Lachen story?
faqs.a: David-Néel's own My Journey to Lhasa and Magic and Mystery in Tibet describe her Sikkim years, including her teacher at Lachen. Several biographies cover the period in detail. Wikipedia's article on her gives a well-referenced summary.

experiences.title: Dusk walk through old Lachen
experiences.cost: Free, or ≈ ₹500 for a local guide
experiences.summary: Before dark on arrival, walk up from the highway hotels into the older part of Lachen, where wooden houses, prayer flags and woodpiles show a village shaped by long winters, herding and its own council. Gentle, short and best with a local host.
body: Most visitors see Lachen only as a strip of hotels on the highway. A short walk uphill leads into the older village: houses of wood and stone with carved window frames, stacks of firewood for the winter, prayer flags and small fields. In the evening, smoke rises from kitchen chimneys and families bring animals in.

Walk slowly. At about 2,750 m, after a long drive, your body is still adjusting, and tomorrow's Gurudongmar trip asks a lot of it. Keep the walk short and gentle, turn back before dark, and carry a torch. Paths can be icy from November to March.

A local host or guide can tell you about the Dzumsa, how the Pipon is chosen, and how the village has coped with years of road closures since 2023. Ask before photographing people and houses, and do not walk into courtyards uninvited.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk around Lachen in the evening?
faqs.a: Yes, Lachen is a quiet, friendly village. Walk before dark, carry a torch, watch for icy patches in winter and loose dogs, and keep the walk short so you are rested for Gurudongmar. Stay on village paths rather than heading into forest or army areas.

faqs.q: What is the Dzumsa of Lachen?
faqs.a: The Dzumsa is Lachen's traditional council, which serves as its local government. It is led by an elected headman, the Pipon, with assistants called Gyenbo. Sikkim law recognises it in place of an ordinary panchayat. It sets village rules, including some for visitors.

faqs.q: Should we rest instead of walking in Lachen?
faqs.a: If you feel tired or have a headache after the drive, rest. A gentle 30–45 minute walk helps many people adjust, but it is not essential. The priority in Lachen is water, a light dinner and an early night before the 4–5 am start.

experiences.title: Yaks, herders and the high pastures
experiences.duration: 1 hour, plus sightings on the Gurudongmar road
experiences.cost: Free with a homestay; tips welcome
experiences.summary: North of Lachen, herders keep yak and sheep on the pastures of Thangu, Chopta, Lashar and Lhonak. Learn from a Lachenpa host how the herding year works, then watch for herds on the drive to Gurudongmar.
body: Yak herding is one of the oldest livelihoods in the upper Lachen valley. Lachenpa families and the Dokpa, a herding community of the high valleys, take yak and sheep up to summer pastures and bring them down as winter closes in. ICIMOD researchers have documented how yak pastoralism in the Lhonak valley is changing, with fewer herders and new pressures from roads, borders and climate.

In a homestay, ask your host about the herding year: when the animals go up, who stays with them, what yak milk becomes (butter, churpi cheese), and how the floods and road closures of recent years affected families. Listen rather than interview; these are livelihoods, not folklore.

On the Gurudongmar drive you will likely see yaks near Thangu, in Chopta Valley and on the plateau. Keep your distance, do not feed them, and ask before photographing herders or their shelters. Some herders on the road charge for photos; agree a price first.

faqs.q: Who are the Dokpa of North Sikkim?
faqs.a: The Dokpa (also written Drokpa) are herders of Tibetan origin who graze yak and sheep in the high valleys north of Lachen, such as Lashar and Lhonak. Wikipedia notes they celebrate a festival with a yak race. Their numbers are small and their areas largely restricted.

faqs.q: Where can we see yaks near Lachen?
faqs.a: Usually not in Lachen itself but higher up: around Thangu, in Chopta Valley and on the plateau towards Gurudongmar, especially from May to November. Herds move with the seasons, so sightings are likely but not guaranteed.

faqs.q: Can we visit a yak herders' camp?
faqs.a: Not as a regular tourist activity. Herders' camps lie in restricted, high areas and are people's workplaces. Watch from the road, greet herders politely and ask before photographing. A homestay host is the best way to learn about herding life.

faqs.q: Is Lachen open for tourists in 2026?
faqs.a: As we understand it, Lachen reopened on 9 March 2026 over a new Bailey bridge on the Taram Chu, closed again in April after a landslide, and permits resumed around 11–12 September 2026 after the road was repaired on 29 August. Check current status before you travel; we confirm before every departure.

faqs.q: How far is Lachen from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 120 km by the North Sikkim Highway via Mangan and Chungthang, usually 5 to 6 hours. Rebuilt stretches after the 2023 flood can be slow. Tourist vehicles must cross the Toong check post by 4:00 pm, so leave Gangtok by 10 am.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Lachen?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian travellers need a protected area permit, issued through a Sikkim Tourism-registered agent with a registered vehicle. Rules for foreign nationals in Lachen and Thangu are unclear at present, and foreigners are not allowed to Gurudongmar. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why stay in Lachen before Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: Gurudongmar is about 67 km beyond Lachen and around 5,150–5,430 m high. Lachen, at about 2,750 m, is the closest village with tourist accommodation and a sensible height to sleep before the climb. You leave around 4–5 am and are back by lunchtime.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Lachen?
faqs.a: About 2,750 m. Sources give figures between roughly 2,700 m and 2,900 m depending on where they measure. Most people feel mild breathlessness at most. Drink water, eat light and avoid alcohol, since the next morning you climb more than 2,000 m.

faqs.q: Can I do Lachen and Lachung in one trip?
faqs.a: Yes, that is the standard 2N/3D or 3N/4D North Sikkim trip: Gangtok to Lachen, Gurudongmar and on to Lachung, then Yumthang and back to Gangtok. The two valleys meet at Chungthang, so you descend from Lachen and climb again to Lachung on day two.

faqs.q: What does a Lachen trip cost?
faqs.a: Indicatively, a shared 2N/3D Lachen–Lachung package from Gangtok costs about ₹7,000–9,500 per person with permit, simple stays and meals. A private SUV for the same trip is about ₹18,000–24,000 per vehicle, plus hotels. Prices rise in May and October.

faqs.q: Is Lachen very cold?
faqs.a: Nights in October and November are close to 0 °C, and from December to February well below freezing, with snow possible. Gurudongmar mornings can be −10 °C or colder with wind. Pack thermals, a down jacket, cap and gloves, even in May.

faqs.q: Can children go to Lachen?
faqs.a: Children under five are not permitted in North Sikkim protected areas, including Lachen and Gurudongmar. Older children can go, but watch them for altitude symptoms, especially on the lake trip. Consider skipping Gurudongmar with younger children and visiting Chopta Valley instead, if permitted.
